title: How to write product descriptions that sell for your online store
summary: Learn how to write product descriptions that sell, and keep them accurate across variants, channels, and product photos with one verified brief.
body_markdown:
**Quick answer:** A product description that sells gives buyers enough verified detail to trust what they're buying: what the product is, why it matters to them, and what they need to know before they buy. Across a catalog, that means writing every version from one product brief of confirmed facts. Generate a draft for each channel with a tool like Photoroom's Product Description Generator, check it against the brief, and make sure the copy matches your product photos.


---


Most advice on writing product descriptions that sell focuses on persuasion: sharper hooks, stronger adjectives. But buyers only act on copy they trust, and trust is hard to maintain when you're writing at scale.


One good description is manageable. Creating hundreds from scratch across variants, channels, and product photos is an operations problem. Under pressure, this is where most catalogs slip: copy gets reused for the wrong variant, the Amazon version drifts from the Shopify one, and the description promises a finish the photos don't show.


When product descriptions aren’t consistent, buyers notice. In a[Photoroom-commissioned survey of 2,000 UK consumers](https://www.photoroom.com/industry-trends/state-of-genai-in-marketplaces-2026) , 63% said variation in product images, styles, or branding across listings makes a seller or marketplace seem unreliable, and 51% said most listings look acceptable but still don't give them full confidence to buy.


**Product descriptions that sell drive credibility, explain relevancy, create confidence, and align with every other element of the product listing, including photos.**


[Photoroom's Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) helps you create that first draft without starting from a blank page, and then apply it across online platforms. You can also use Photoroom to prepare the product visuals around the product description, so the copy and imagery represent the same product before you publish.


This guide walks through that workflow: building a product brief, generating and reviewing a first draft with the Product Description Generator, improving the output, optimizing it for search and AI discovery, adapting it across channels, and creating images that support the copy.


## Table of Contents


## How to create a product brief as your source of truth


A product brief is a single record of what's true about a product. You write it once and use it for every channel, variant, and person who works on the product description. When the Amazon version, the Shopify version, and[the navy variant](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-variant-image-generation) all come from the same brief, they can differ in tone and structure without contradicting each other.


Build the brief from facts and evidence, not adjectives. Words like "beautiful," "premium," and "versatile" feel persuasive, but they don't answer the questions shoppers have before buying. Shoppers can't pick up the product or try it on, so the description has to answer those questions for them.


### Start with the questions shoppers already ask


Customer reviews, support messages, return reasons, and pre-purchase questions can help identify what deserves priority:


-


If shoppers keep asking whether a phone case fits their model, list the compatible models near the top of the description.


-


If a shirt gets returned because it runs small, the listing needs a clear sizing note and a pointer to the size chart.


-


If buyers ask whether a mug can go in the dishwasher, the care instructions belong in the listing.


Each repeated question tells you which fact to prioritize, and each repeated return tells you which fact is missing or unclear.


### Record what your images already show


The product description and the product images work together, so note which aspects of the product the photos show. Whatever the images can't show is what the description has to carry. Whatever they do show, the copy should agree with.


### Organize product facts into a brief


With those inputs, the brief itself can be simple:


Input What to record Example (Linen shirt)


Product facts Verified material, size, fit, capacity, compatibility, included items, care or setup information, or other specifications 100% linen; relaxed fit; long sleeves; mother-of-pearl buttons; machine washable; sizes XS–XL; white, sand, and navy


Buyer need What the buyer wants the product to help them do A lightweight shirt for warm weather that works with jeans or tailored trousers


Differentiator A meaningful reason this product is different Mother-of-pearl buttons on a relaxed cut


Objection What could make someone hesitate Runs slightly small; customers ask whether to size up


Proof The specification, construction detail, or other evidence supporting the benefit Garment measurements for each size (chest width, length, sleeve length) and fabric composition from the supplier spec sheet


Visual evidence What the product images already show Front, back, and on-model shots, plus a button close-up. The photos don't show how the fit compares with the buyer's usual size, so the copy has to.


Claims to avoid Statements that sound appealing but can't be verified, or that contradict the product facts "Wrinkle-resistant" (linen creases naturally); "true to size" (contradicts the sizing feedback); "sustainable" or "eco-friendly" without a certification to back it up


The last row is the one that protects your listings. Writing down what's off-limits gives you something concrete to check every draft against. It also helps anyone else who writes a listing for the same product or a new variant later.


This gives you a source of truth whether you write the description manually or generate it with AI.


## How to generate a first draft with Photoroom's Product Description Generator


[Photoroom's Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) helps turn product information into a first draft. Generic AI tools require you to write the prompt, explain the desired output, and know each platform’s rules. But the Product Description Generator is built for e‑commerce—any small business can use it to generate detailed drafts, without a specific prompt or specialized knowledge.


### Choose the channel of your online store


[Different platforms and marketplaces](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/multichannel-product-image-optimization) have different requirements for product descriptions.


[Amazon](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/sell-on-amazon) , for example, restricts promotional language such as “best seller” and caps description length, while[eBay](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/sell-on-ebay) allows much longer descriptions but truncates them on mobile.[Shopify](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/sell-on-shopify) has no fixed limit, so the description follows your store's own formatting.


Start by selecting where the description will be published: Shopify, Amazon, Etsy, eBay, or a generic marketplace option. When generating the copy, Photoroom applies that platform's character limits, formatting, and content rules.


### Enter your product details


Paste in facts from the brief: the product name, then the verified specifications (materials, dimensions, fit, capacity, or compatibility), the buyer need, the differentiator, the objection you want to answer, the proof behind each benefit, and the claims to avoid.


If the copy needs to support a claim the corresponding image can’t, note it here, too. The more thorough product information you start with, the more useful the generated draft can be.


###


### Set your brand voice


For brand voice, specific guidance is also more useful than “make it sound on-brand.” Here’s an example of a strong brand voice prompt:


**Direct, warm, and practical. Short sentences. No exaggerated superlatives. Use “purse” rather than “bag”.**


You can provide this information or select a pre-created brand voice descriptor from the drop-down menu. Using a single predetermined brand voice can create additional consistency when multiple people generate product descriptions.


### Choose the length


[The Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) allows you to choose a length for the output. There’s no universal ideal length for product descriptions, but a general rule of thumb is:


-


**Choose short** when the product is familiar and low-risk, and the photos already show most of what buyers need to know.


-


**Choose medium** when buyers have one or two specific questions to answer before they'll buy, such as sizing, care, or a single compatibility point.


-


**Choose long** when the product is technical, unfamiliar, or compatible with many models, or when a higher price means buyers need more reassurance.


For example, a stoneware mug or a basic tee only needs a few lines plus a specs block. A kitchen appliance or an electronic accessory that works with several compatible devices usually needs additional copy.


### Review for accuracy


AI-generated copy can sound convincing even when it’s making a statement that hasn’t been verified. Check materials, dimensions, compatibility, certifications, included items, performance claims, and product benefits against your source information. If you can’t verify a statement, remove or qualify it.


Then check the draft against your product photos. If the copy says "lightly textured" and the close-up shows a smooth, glossy glaze, one of them is wrong. Fix whichever doesn't match the product. For product descriptions that describe variants without associated images, you can use a tool like[Photoroom’s Recolor tool](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) to create accurate variants from a source image.


## How to make product descriptions more useful and relevant to shoppers


An accurate listing isn't automatically a strong one. Where information appears and how it's phrased affect whether buyers understand what they're buying, why it's relevant to them, and how it differs from similar products.


Ask these questions of every draft:


-


Does the opening identify the product quickly?


-


Are there generic phrases that could be used by competitors?


-


Is the important buyer information forward?


-


Does the description explain why certain specifications matter?


That last question is where many product descriptions fall short. A specification on its own is a fact. It becomes useful when the copy connects it to what the buyer needs:


-


**Feature:** 500 ml insulated bottle


-


**Buyer relevance:** Holds a standard serving and reduces the need for frequent refills.


A useful description combines both:


The 500 ml capacity holds a standard serving, while the insulated construction helps slow temperature change between refills.


###


### When you should edit vs. when you should regenerate product descriptions


When an AI-generated draft needs work, decide whether the problem is in the draft or the product brief. If the problem is in the inputs, fixing it by hand only fixes this one version. The same issue will come back in every channel and variant you generate from those inputs.


Draft issue How to fix it


Sounds off-brand throughout Tighten the brand voice prompt or choose a different brand voice setting then regenerate


Too long or too short for the product Choose a different length and regenerate


Doesn't answer the buyer's main hesitation Add the objection to the product brief and regenerate


Emphasizes the wrong feature Move the key fact higher in your product brief, or state the buyer need more clearly then regenerate


Has one awkward phrase or sentence Edit by hand


Includes a single unverified claim Remove it by hand and add it to the brief's claims-to-avoid row if it keeps appearing


As a rule, edit by hand for one-off wording problems, and regenerate when the problem will repeat. Once the inputs are right, every version generated from them starts in better shape.


## How to optimize product descriptions for search and AI discovery


The product description is one of the main sources of text that search engines and[AI shopping tools](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/chatgpt-shopping) use to work out what a product is, who it's for, and which searches it should appear in.


A useful SEO product description should make the product easy for search engines and AI shopping systems to identify. That shouldn’t mean the copy turns into a collection of keywords. Name the product naturally near the beginning and include relevant language around its material, use case, audience, style, or compatibility where those attributes are accurate.


For example, “350 ml handmade stoneware mug” simultaneously identifies the product, gives shoppers useful information, and aligns with a specific search query.


Clear product facts can[make listings easier for AI shopping systems to interpret](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/ai-catalog-readiness-checklist) . Product identity, attributes, variants, and use cases should be explicit and consistent rather than hidden inside vague marketing language.


When you generate a draft with the[Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) , include your target keywords alongside the product facts you enter, such as "linen shirt for women" or "relaxed-fit linen shirt." Only include keywords that describe the product accurately. The generator works from what you give it, so a keyword for a feature the product doesn't have can end up in the draft as a claim.


[Images are part of that search, too.](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/ai-systems-product-images) Search engines read image alt text and file names, and visual search tools let shoppers search using a photo instead of words. Describe each image accurately in its alt text, using the same product name and attributes as the copy. When the words and images describe the same product, the listing sends a single consistent signal.


Clear product information can support machine understanding, but it doesn’t guarantee that a product will appear or be recommended in an[AI shopping experience](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/chatgpt-shopping) .


## How to adapt product descriptions across channels and variants


Forty products in three colors on three channels is 360 descriptions. Written from scratch, that's 360 chances for a fact to slip. Built from product briefs, it's 40 sources of truth, with each version generated from a brief rather than copied from the last listing.


You don't need to reinvent the product story for every channel or color. Start with the same verified product information, then[adapt how it's presented for each marketplace](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-variant-image-generation) , and update only the facts that actually change between variants.


### Adapting for channels


A Shopify description may have more room for distinctive brand language, while an Amazon listing may surface specifications and compatibility sooner. Neither should suddenly describe a different material, size, included component, or use case.


Channel What to emphasize


Shopify or your online store Brand voice, use cases, benefits, and scannable product facts


Amazon Important specifications, benefits, compatibility, and current category requirements


Etsy Materials, maker context, process, gifting, and relevant natural variation


eBay Condition, item specifics, compatibility, and what's included, with the key details near the top for mobile shoppers


To create each channel version, go back to the brief, enter the same facts in the[Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) , and select a different marketplace. The generator adjusts the structure, length, and emphasis to suit that channel and applies its character limits and content rules.


Then review each version against the brief itself, not the version before it, so a mistake in one doesn't carry into the next. Platform and category requirements change, so check the current rules before publishing.


###


### Adapting for variants


Variants are where copied descriptions do the most damage. Duplicating a listing and swapping the color name takes seconds, but if anything else differs between variants, the new listing is wrong.


Before generating a description for a new variant, split the brief into two groups: fields that stay the same and fields that change, like color name, color-specific care instructions, and the product images.


Update the fields that change, then[generate the variant's description](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) from the updated brief.[Each variant also needs its own photos](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-product-color-variants-without-reshooting) , and the color name in the copy has to match what the images show.


If a variant differs in more than color or size, such as a heavier fabric, a cropped cut, or different buttons, treat it as a separate product with its own brief. A copied description that's 90% right is still wrong, and the 10% that's off is usually what gets the product returned.


## How to create images that support your product description


Your existing images should display what’s stated in your product description. This is[product fidelity](https://www.photoroom.com/glossary/fidelity) : when images and text align to create one product truth. But beyond your standard listing photos, you might need additional images to illustrate what the copy can’t.


Copy is better at explaining:


-


Exact dimensions


-


Materials


-


Compatibility


-


Care and setup


-


Included and excluded items


-


Limitations


-


Benefits that require context


Images are usually better at showing:


-


Appearance and color


-


Texture and finish


-


Construction


-


Components


-


Relative scale


-


The product in use


So, **if your description emphasizes compact size** , you might show a credible scale reference in the photos. **If texture or craftsmanship matters** , include a detail image. **If the product is designed for a particular setting** , an[accurate lifestyle image](https://www.photoroom.com/ai-product-photography/lifestyle) can communicate that more effectively than another paragraph of copy.


Only create images that address a genuine buyer question or need. Generating additional images without a clear purpose only adds to your workload and doesn’t necessarily improve the quality of your product descriptions or listings.


Photoroom can help prepare this visual side of the listing through tools for background removal, product staging, resizing, and other product-image workflows. Create clean primary images with[Background Remover](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) , show the product in a lifestyle scene with[Product Staging](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-staging) , and resize the image for use across channels with[Image Resizer](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/image-resizer) and[AI Expand](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/ai-expand) .


Generated or edited imagery still needs to accurately represent the real product. Check color, proportions, materials, patterns, logos, components, packaging, and variants against the product the customer will receive.


## How to create product descriptions that sell online: a checklist


Run through this checklist before any listing goes live, including new variants and channel versions. It checks the finished listing as a whole because buyers evaluate the words and the images together.


### Copy


-


**The product is identified in the first line** , including its defining attribute (for example, "350 ml handmade stoneware mug").


-


**Every specification matches the brief** : materials, measurements, capacity, fit, compatibility, and included items.


-


**Every benefit is backed by a verifiable fact** . Claims you can't verify, such as certifications or performance figures, are removed or qualified.


-


**The buyer's main objection is answered** , whether that's sizing, fit, compatibility, or care.


-


**Keywords read naturally** . No features have been added just because people search for them.


-


**The copy is distinct** . No generic phrases that could describe any competitor, and no copied manufacturer text.


### Channels and variants


-


**Each version was**[generated for the right marketplace](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/multichannel-product-image-optimization) and meets that category's current requirements.


-


**The product facts are identical across every channel version** . Only structure, length, and emphasis differ.


-


**Variant-specific fields are updated** : color name, size, model, and any care notes. Nothing is carried over from another variant.


### Images


-


**The primary image** meets the marketplace's main-image requirements.


-


**Edited or**[generated images match the real product](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-fix-inaccurate-ai-product-images) : color, proportions, materials, patterns, logos, components, and packaging.


-


[Each variant has its own images](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-variant-image-generation) , not a photo of a different color or model.


-


**Every claim is either shown in a photo or stated in the specs** . Nothing asks the buyer to take it on trust.


### Images and copy together


-


**Color names in the copy match the images** for every variant.


-


**Descriptions of texture and finish match the close-ups** . "Lightly textured" shouldn't sit next to a smooth, glossy photo.


-


**The scale shot supports the stated size** , dimensions, or capacity.


-


**The "Includes" line matches what the images suggest** . If a photo shows accessories or props that don't ship with the product, the copy says so.


## Create product descriptions that sell online with Photoroom


A product description sells when buyers trust it. That trust doesn't come from sharper hooks or stronger adjectives. It comes from a listing that's accurate about the product, describes the same product across every channel, and matches the photos next to it.


Across a growing catalog, that consistency depends more on your workflow than on your writing. Start with one verified brief per product. Use[Photoroom's Product Description Generator](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-description-generator) to turn it into a first draft for Shopify, Amazon, Etsy, or eBay, with each platform's character limits and content rules applied. When you add a channel or a variant, generate again from the same brief instead of rewriting, and review each version against the brief rather than against the last one.


Then make sure the images tell the same story. Create clean primary images with[Background Remover](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/background-remover) , show the product in use with[Product Staging](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/product-staging) , and create accurate images for every variant with[AI product photography](https://www.photoroom.com/ai-product-photography) and[recolor tools](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) .
